question: to the Commission Catherine Griset (PfE) Subject:

On 15 June 2026, the US administration ordered Anthropic to block foreign nationals, including those living in the US, from accessing its best AI models: Mythos 5 and its restricted version, Fable 5. However, since Anthropic could not determine the nationality of its users with any certainty, it decided to disable its models for all customers1. Collateral victims of this decision, European companies and users have thus been put in a difficult position, revealing our dependence on the policy decisions of non-EU countries that are much more advanced with regard to digital technology. That dependence could increase in light of recent developments in China, which also has plans to limit global access to its most advanced AI models2. 1.
Given the risk of EU companies being cut off at any moment from the world’s leading AI models, is the Commission ready to boost the development of European AI models, which are few and far between?
Will there be priority access for European AI in public procurement in the EU?
Will the requirement to process EU data within our internal market be gradually implemented?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (7.9.2026) The Commission is committed to strengthening the development of European AI models. Through the AI Continent Action Plan1 and the InvestAI initiative2, it supports European AI developers and the infrastructure they require. Recently, it launched a call for tenders for AI Gigafactories, supported by up to EUR 10 billion in public funding and expected to unlock at least EUR 20 billion in private investment for developing advanced AI models on European infrastructure3. The European Frontier AI Initiative complements these efforts to enhance the Union’s competitiveness, sovereignty and security in frontier AI. The Cloud and AI Development Act (CADA)4, proposed by the Commission as part of the Tech Sovereignty package5, promotes sovereign services and EU added value. It obliges contracting authorities to include criteria in the procurement of cloud computing services and AI systems rewarding local innovation and supply chain resilience. Furthermore, CADA introduces a single EU-wide sovereignty framework for cloud computing services based on four assurance levels. Highly critical public sector activities will have to rely on the suitable assurance levels. The highest assurance levels are easier to attain for EU AI providers as it is more straightforward for them to demonstrate conformity with several of the sovereignty requirements, notably the absence of third-country influence. Every EU assurance level under the CADA proposal requires customer data to in principle remain exclusively within the EU. This requirement applies to all cloud computing services supplied to public sector bodies.
